title: STS 2026 Guidelines: Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation After Cardiac Surgery
breakthrough: The Society of Thoracic Surgeons published clinical practice guidelines for the prevention and treatment of new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation after CARDIAC surgery, developed by the STS Workforce on Evidence-Based Surgery. Fifteen recommendations are organised into three domains: perioperative interventions to reduce POAF, intraoperative strategies to prevent it, and postoperative treatment. The guidance is notably more assertive about amiodarone and posterior pericardiotomy than prior practice. POAF is the most frequent complication after cardiac surgery and carries greater morbidity, mortality, length of stay and cost.
impact: A phase-based framework replaces the piecemeal habit of treating POAF as a postoperative surprise. Naming preoperative and intraoperative prevention as separate domains puts the decision before the arrhythmia rather than after it.
practical: Note the scope: these are cardiac surgery guidelines. POAF after lung resection or esophagectomy is a related but distinct problem with its own incidence and its own evidence base, and the recommendations here should not be transplanted wholesale to a thoracic service. Posterior pericardiotomy is the intervention most likely to be new to a unit — it is an intraoperative decision, so it has to be discussed before the case, not on the ward round afterwards. The anticoagulation question for POAF persisting beyond 48 hours is genuinely unsettled and is treated separately in this list.
link: The Society of Thoracic Surgeons 2026 clinical practice guidelines for the prevention and treatment of new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery

title: 2026 Multisociety Guideline for Acute Pulmonary Embolism
journal: Circulation / Journal of the American College of Cardiology
breakthrough: The first ACC/AHA clinical practice guideline on acute pulmonary embolism, written jointly with ACCP, ACEP, CHEST, SCAI, SHM, SIR, SVM and SVN. Its central innovation is a new classification, the Acute Pulmonary Embolism Clinical Categories, with five categories A through E plus subcategories, spanning low to high risk of adverse outcomes, intended to sharpen severity classification, prognosis and treatment selection. At the low end, patients in Category A can be discharged home from the emergency department without hospitalisation.
impact: Ten societies signing one document ends a long period in which emergency physicians, cardiologists, interventional radiologists and surgeons each risk-stratified PE differently. A shared category is what makes a PE response team conversation coherent.
practical: For a thoracic surgeon the relevant end is the high-severity one, where surgical embolectomy competes with catheter-directed therapy and systemic thrombolysis. The categories are a common language for that discussion, not an algorithm that selects the intervention — the choice still turns on haemodynamics, right ventricular function, bleeding risk, clot location and what the institution can actually deliver at 3am. Learn the category definitions from the guideline itself rather than from a summary: the whole benefit is that everyone in the room means the same thing by 'Category C'.
link: 2026 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ACEP/CHEST/SCAI/SHM/SIR/SVM/SVN guideline for the evaluation and management of acute pulmonary embolism in adults

verify.status: matched with corrections — guideline and categories verified, journals and specifics adjusted
verify.note: Verified: the 2026 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ACEP/CHEST/SCAI/SHM/SIR/SVM/SVN guideline, published in Circulation (CIR.0000000000001415) and JACC, is the first ACC/AHA guideline on acute PE and does introduce 'Acute Pulmonary Embolism Clinical Categories' with five categories A–E plus subcategories, ranging low to high risk. The submission's URL is correct. Corrections. (1) The submission says it was 'published across Circulation, CHEST, and JAMA'; it appears in Circulation and JACC — CHEST is one of the ten writing societies, not a journal of publication, and JAMA is not involved. (2) The submission's specific operational claims — 'fast-track home discharge for low-risk presentations' and 'expediting thoracic surgical embolectomy consultation for category D/E incipient cardiopulmonary collapse' — are directionally plausible and the Category A home-discharge point is verifiable, but the D/E-to-embolectomy mapping could not be confirmed and is now stated as the discussion the categories enable rather than as a guideline instruction. (3) 'Replaces rigid risk scores' overstates it; the categories are a new scheme, and existing scores are not withdrawn.

title: STS 2026: Nodal Assessment, Upstaging and Survival in Node-Negative NSCLC
journal: Society of Thoracic Surgeons Annual Meeting (J. Maxwell Chamberlain Memorial Paper)
breakthrough: Christopher Seder presented the J. Maxwell Chamberlain Memorial Paper in General Thoracic Surgery on 31 January 2026: an STS National Database analysis of 48,779 patients with clinically node-negative NSCLC, examining the association between nodal assessment, upstaging and survival. 11.2% were upstaged after surgery — their nodal dissection revealed more advanced disease than clinical staging had shown. North American surgical standards set in 2021 call for assessment of three N2 mediastinal stations plus one N1 hilar node; the study's recommendation is that MORE THAN ONE N1 node be removed and examined.
impact: One in nine clinically node-negative patients has occult nodal disease found only by the dissection. Those are the patients who become candidates for adjuvant chemoimmunotherapy or targeted therapy — and who do not, if the nodes are not taken.
practical: The actionable change is narrower and easier than a wholesale new quality metric: sample more than one N1 node. Hilar nodes are the ones most often taken as a single specimen or skipped when the lobectomy has gone quickly, and they are where this study locates the shortfall. Upstaging is not a complication — it is the operation working, and it should be framed that way to a patient who asks why their stage changed after surgery. Label and submit each station separately; a pooled specimen loses the station-level information the adjuvant decision depends on.
link: STS 2026 — association between nodal assessment, upstaging and survival in resected clinically node-negative NSCLC

verify.status: corrected — upstaging rate and nodal threshold both wrong
verify.note: The presentation is real: Seder, J. Maxwell Chamberlain Memorial Paper in General Thoracic Surgery, STS 2026 Annual Meeting, 31 January 2026, STS National Database, 48,779 clinically node-negative NSCLC patients. Three corrections. (1) UPSTAGING: the submission says extended sampling 'alters pathologic staging in up to 14% of cT1-T2' cases; the reported figure is 11.2%. (2) THRESHOLD: the submission specifies '>10 nodes across at least 3 N2 stations'. The 2021 North American standard is three N2 stations plus one N1 node, and this study's actual recommendation is that more than one N1 node be removed — a specific, modest change, not a ten-node count. A fabricated numerical threshold in a quality metric is the kind of detail that gets audited against, so it has been replaced with what was presented. (3) The submission claims the work 'establishes stricter quality benchmarks... PENALIZING non-systematic sampling in quality metrics'; no such penalty exists — this is a presented database analysis, not an adopted metric. Also restated as a conference presentation rather than 'a trial', and added the practical point the submission omitted: stations must be submitted separately for the finding to be usable.

title: Resection Without Preoperative Tissue Diagnosis in Indeterminate Nodules
journal: Multiple (surgical series and CHEST nodule guidance)
breakthrough: Preoperative tissue diagnosis is not always obtainable, and operating without it is accepted practice within limits. For indeterminate solid lesions of 8–30 mm, management follows the pretest probability of malignancy, with surgical resection recommended for high-probability lesions — above roughly 65% — ideally as thoracoscopic wedge resection with intraoperative frozen section. The benign yield in published series quantifies the cost: of 500 consecutive resections without preoperative tissue diagnosis, 336 (67.2%) were lung cancer, 93 (18.6%) metastatic cancer and 71 (14.2%) benign. In a series of 199 patients resected without a definitive preoperative diagnosis, 98 (49%) went to upfront lobectomy without frozen section because wedge resection was not feasible, and 6% of those proved benign. Male sex, increasing age, smoking history and prior lung cancer predict malignancy.
impact: The framing that matters is that proceeding without tissue is a probability decision with a quantified benign rate, not a shortcut. Roughly one in seven resections done this way removes something benign.
practical: The rule that protects patients is about the magnitude of what is being committed: a diagnostic thoracoscopic wedge with frozen section is a reasonable way to resolve a high-probability nodule, and an anatomical resection should follow only once malignancy is confirmed. A lobectomy or pneumonectomy without a tissue diagnosis is a different proposition — the 6% benign rate in the upfront-lobectomy series is the price, and for a pneumonectomy it is not an acceptable one. Where the nodule is deep and transthoracic needle aspiration carries a high pneumothorax risk, navigational bronchoscopy or an intraoperative approach is the better route to tissue, not abandoning the tissue requirement.
link: Lung resection without tissue diagnosis: a pragmatic perspective on the indeterminate pulmonary nodule

verify.status: NOT FOUND as cited — no STS 2026 guideline on this exists; rebuilt from the real evidence
verify.note: The submission attributes this to 'STS 2026 guidelines' that 'established clear benchmarks permitting surgical resection without a preoperative tissue biopsy in select high-risk indeterminate pulmonary nodules', with a link to a generic STS topic page. No such 2026 guideline could be found. The underlying clinical position IS well established but comes from surgical series and pulmonary nodule guidance, not a new document: pretest probability above roughly 65% supports resection, ideally thoracoscopic wedge; benign rates in resection-without-diagnosis series are 14.2% (500 patients) and 6% in an upfront-lobectomy subset. Entry rebuilt on those sources. The submission's own instinct — that high-risk diagnostic manoeuvres in deep lesions and pneumonectomy without tissue should be rejected — is sound and has been kept and sharpened, because the graded rule (wedge with frozen section yes, anatomical resection only after confirmation, pneumonectomy never) is the part that actually protects a patient and the submission stated it only loosely.

title: Reoperative Surgical Mitral Valve Replacement Versus Transcatheter Valve-in-Valve
breakthrough: A retrospective cohort at two quaternary care centres compared transcatheter mitral valve-in-valve (mViV) against reoperative surgical mitral valve replacement (rSMVR) for failing bioprosthetic mitral valves without active endocarditis, 2004 to 2023. Of 229 patients — 90 rSMVR, 139 mViV, mean age 66.0 versus 68.7 years — 30-day Mitral Valve Academic Research Consortium outcomes were similar between groups except for more prolonged ventilation after surgery. Endpoints were 30-day MVARC procedural success and five-year cumulative incidence of death, freedom from reintervention and heart failure. The reported long-term signal favours reoperative surgery.
impact: Transcatheter valve-in-valve is established as safe in the short term, and the open question has been what happens over years. A cohort with follow-up long enough to reach five years begins to answer it, and the answer favours the open operation in patients who can tolerate one.
practical: This is 229 patients at two high-volume centres, retrospectively compared, over a nineteen-year period during which both technologies changed substantially — so it identifies a direction, not an effect size to quote. The clinically defensible reading is the one the numbers support: mViV has the gentler early course, rSMVR the better long-term trajectory, so age and operative risk should drive the choice. A younger low-to-intermediate-risk patient with a failed bioprosthesis is the one for whom accepting a redo sternotomy plausibly buys durability; a frail high-risk patient is who valve-in-valve exists for. Beware the selection built into the comparison: the patients who were offered surgery in this cohort were offered it because someone judged they would survive it.
link: Long-term survival advantage of reoperative surgical mitral valve replacement over transcatheter mitral valve-in-valve: a multicenter cohort

verify.status: corrected — study design and follow-up horizon both overstated
verify.note: The study is real: Annals of Thoracic Surgery, published April 2026 (S0003-4975(26)00250-X), presented at the Thirty-third Annual Meeting of the Asian Society for Cardiovascular and Thoracic Surgery in May 2025, and its title does report a long-term survival advantage for reoperative surgery. Three corrections. (1) DESIGN: the submission calls it 'a large multi-center REGISTRY TRIAL'. It is a RETROSPECTIVE COHORT of 229 patients at TWO quaternary centres — not large, not a registry, not a trial. (2) FOLLOW-UP: the submission cites 'durable 10-year survival'; the published endpoints are five-year cumulative incidence of death, reintervention and heart failure. (3) The submission's claim of 'lower initial perioperative morbidity (transcatheter)' is partly supported — 30-day MVARC outcomes were SIMILAR except for more prolonged ventilation after surgery, which is narrower than a general morbidity advantage. Added the selection-bias caveat, which is decisive in a retrospective comparison of an operation against a catheter procedure, and the point that both technologies evolved across the 2004–2023 study window.

title: Extended Arch Versus Hemiarch Replacement in Older Patients With Type A Dissection
breakthrough: A retrospective cohort from the Shizuoka Kokuho Database — a Japanese prefecture-wide, multi-institutional administrative claims database — identified patients aged 60 or older with acute type A aortic dissection who underwent hemiarch or extended arch replacement between April 2012 and September 2022. Of 774 patients (174 extended arch, 600 hemiarch), 167 propensity-matched pairs were analysed, and Kaplan-Meier curves showed no significant difference in survival between the procedures. Wider meta-analytic data — 23 observational studies, 4,576 patients — find hemiarch associated with lower early mortality, less permanent neurological dysfunction and less dialysis-requiring renal failure, but a HIGHER rate of late mortality.
impact: In older patients, matched analysis shows no survival penalty for the less extensive operation. Given that hemiarch carries lower early mortality and less neurological injury, that supports the simpler repair as the default when the dissection anatomy allows it.
practical: Two facts have to sit together rather than be chosen between: hemiarch is safer early, and across the broader literature it carries a higher late mortality — the matched elderly cohort finds no survival difference, which is the specific circumstance in which the trade-off resolves in favour of the simpler operation. That resolution is age-dependent, so do not carry it to a 45-year-old, where late reintervention on a residual dissected arch is the dominant risk. The extent of repair still follows the anatomy: an arch tear or a dissection extending well into the arch is not a hemiarch. Claims-database data cannot see tear location, so this study cannot tell you which patients needed the bigger operation.
link: Comparison of extended arch versus hemiarch replacement in elderly patients with type A aortic dissection: the Shizuoka Kokuho Database

verify.status: corrected — right conclusion, wrong registry, wrong forum, wrong age cut-off
verify.note: The finding of no survival difference is confirmed, but nothing about the attribution was correct. The study is Arima, Sato and Tanaka, Interdisciplinary CardioVascular and Thoracic Surgery, published 10 January 2026, volume 41 issue 1, ivag017 — a retrospective analysis of the SHIZUOKA KOKUHO DATABASE, a Japanese prefecture-wide administrative CLAIMS database, in patients aged ≥60, 774 patients with 167 propensity-matched pairs. The submission describes 'a prospective STS registry study presented at STS 2026' in 'patients over 65'. Every one of those is wrong: not STS, not prospective, not presented at STS 2026, and the age threshold is 60. The submission also claims identical 'reintervention rates', which was not among the verified outcomes, and asserts the finding 'slashes operative hypothermic circulatory arrest times and lowers perioperative stroke' — those come from the separate meta-analysis (23 studies, 4,576 patients), which ALSO found hemiarch carries HIGHER LATE MORTALITY, a counterweight the submission omitted entirely. Both sides are now stated, along with the reason the trade-off resolves differently by age and the limitation that claims data cannot see tear location.

title: Diaphragm Dysfunction After Congenital Heart Surgery: Epidemiology and Outcomes
journal: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
breakthrough: An analysis of 77,383 patients undergoing an index congenital cardiac operation identified diaphragm dysfunction in 1,130 (1.5%), of whom 510 (45%) underwent plication. Median day of diagnosis was postoperative day 7 (IQR 4–13) and median day of plication was postoperative day 14 (IQR 9–24). Patients with diaphragm dysfunction had longer mechanical ventilation, more major complications and longer cardiac ICU and hospital stays. Patients who underwent plication did not have higher rates of major complications — the procedure itself was not associated with added harm.
impact: It puts numbers on a complication that has been managed by local habit: 1.5% incidence, diagnosis around a week, plication around two weeks, and just under half of affected infants operated on. The morbidity attributable to diaphragm dysfunction itself is substantial.
practical: What this study does NOT show is that plicating earlier improves outcomes, and the wider evidence cautions against assuming it. A comparison of aggressive early plication against conservative management found no significant difference in ventilation time (6 versus 8 days, P=0.36), and plicated and non-plicated patients regained diaphragm function at similar rates (60% versus 54.8%); excursion of a plicated diaphragm reaches about 77% of the contralateral side. So the honest position is that plication is safe and reasonable in an infant who cannot be weaned, and that it is not established to shorten ventilation compared with waiting for recovery. Diagnose it deliberately — the median postoperative day 7 detection suggests it is often found late, on a failed wean rather than looked for.
link: Diaphragm dysfunction following congenital heart surgery: epidemiology and outcomes

verify.status: REVERSED on benefit — a descriptive epidemiology study was presented as proving early plication works
verify.note: The study is real and its figures check out: 77,383 index operations, 1,130 (1.5%) with diaphragm dysfunction, 510 (45%) plicated, median diagnosis POD 7, median plication POD 14, worse ventilation/complications/length of stay with dysfunction, no excess major complications from plication itself. But the submission's conclusions do not follow from it. (1) It is described as 'a 77,000+-patient TRIAL' — it is an epidemiology and outcomes analysis. (2) The submission says it 'defines standardized criteria for early diaphragmatic plication'; the paper describes current practice, it does not set criteria. (3) The submission claims plication 'DRAMATICALLY DECREASES ventilator days, pediatric ICU stay lengths, and tracheostomy rates'. That comparison was not made here, and separate published evidence points the other way: no significant ventilation-time difference between aggressive early plication and conservative management (6 vs 8 days, P=0.36), similar functional recovery in plicated and non-plicated patients (60% vs 54.8%), and plicated diaphragm excursion at 77% of the contralateral side. Since the entry as submitted would push a surgeon toward operating on an infant on the belief that a large study proved benefit, the actual evidence has been stated in full. The genuinely reassuring finding — plication did not add major complications — is retained. Note the submission's typo 'unable to weed from mechanical ventilation'.

title: COVID-19-Positive Donor Hearts in Pediatric Transplantation: Three-Year Outcomes
journal: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
breakthrough: A query of the Standard Transplant Analysis and Research database covering primary paediatric (under 18) heart transplants from 2020 to 2024 identified 1,978 transplants, of which 60 (3.0%) used COVID-19-positive donor hearts. Three-year survival was 71.5% for recipients of COVID-19-positive hearts against 86.3% for COVID-19-negative. Mortality did not differ at 6 months, 1 year or 1.5 years — the divergence appeared only at 2 and 3 years. Recipients of positive hearts were younger (5.7 versus 7.6 years, P=.019), received organs from greater distances (360 versus 303 miles, P=.044) and had more peritransplant ECMO use. Mortality risk was magnified by height mismatch (P=.048). Graft failure was rare and its cumulative risk was not significant.
impact: A nearly 15-percentage-point survival gap at three years in a population that should be doing well, with no signal at all in the first eighteen months, is the kind of late divergence a shorter study would have declared safe.
practical: The authors' own conclusion is the right one to carry: until more data accrue, exercise caution in accepting COVID-19-positive donor hearts for paediatric recipients. Read the late timing as a warning about follow-up length rather than as a mechanism — that graft failure was rare while mortality rose means the deaths are not straightforwardly explained by the graft, and the confounders in the table (younger recipients, longer distances, more ECMO) describe sicker children receiving organs under more pressure. Height mismatch amplified the risk, so the combination of a positive donor and a size mismatch is the one to decline. This is registry data on 60 exposed patients: it is a reason for caution, not a prohibition, and the decision is still made against the mortality of remaining on the waiting list.
link: Clinical outcomes after COVID-19-positive donor heart transplantation in the United States pediatric population

verify.status: matched with corrections — figures exact, guideline claim invented
verify.note: Verified precisely: 1,978 paediatric transplants 2020–2024 from the Standard Transplant Analysis and Research database, 60 (3.0%) COVID-19-positive donors, three-year survival 71.5% versus 86.3%. The submission's two survival figures are exactly right. Corrections. (1) The submission claims the study 'REWRITES ISHLT and UNOS pediatric organ acceptance guidelines, placing strict restrictions on donor height mismatches and ISCHEMIC TIMES'. No guideline change could be found; the paper's stated conclusion is that transplant teams should exercise caution pending more data. Ischaemic time was not among the identified risk modifiers — HEIGHT MISMATCH was (P=.048) — so one of the two named restrictions is not in the paper at all. (2) The submission asserts the finding protects recipients 'from LATE GRAFT LOSS'; graft failure was explicitly rare with non-significant cumulative risk, so the mortality is not attributable to graft loss on these data. Corrected. Added the timing pattern (no difference to 1.5 years, divergence at 2–3 years), the baseline imbalances that confound it, and the small exposed denominator — all omitted from the submission and all necessary to weigh a decision that is made against waiting-list mortality.

title: DIPNECH and Multifocal Pulmonary Neuroendocrine Disease: No Guideline Exists
breakthrough: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia is an idiopathic proliferation of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells that causes bronchiolitis and can give rise to multifocal lung neuroendocrine tumours, typically presenting with chronic cough and dyspnoea. There are NO evidence-based management guidelines. Somatostatin analogues can palliate symptoms, particularly cough. Surgical resection is considered for individual larger — for example above 1 cm — progressive carcinoid tumours, and published surgical experience consists of case reports and small series of wedge resections or lobectomy.
impact: The honest state of the field is the finding here. DIPNECH is a diffuse airway process; the resectable component is the discrete carcinoid tumour that arises within it, not the hyperplasia itself, and there is no series large enough to define a surgical algorithm.
practical: Framing matters because the disease is diffuse and indolent: resection treats a specific progressive nodule, it does not treat DIPNECH, and a patient whose dominant problem is cough is more likely to be helped by a somatostatin analogue than by an operation. Because the process is bilateral and multifocal, every resection spends parenchyma the patient may need for a future one — which is a strong argument for the most limited adequate resection and a strong argument against a large one. Multidisciplinary review with a neuroendocrine tumour service, serial imaging, and treating the airway disease medically is the defensible pathway; the absence of guidelines means the burden of justification sits on the decision to operate, not on the decision to wait.
link: An update on the management of diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)

verify.status: NOT FOUND — no such series or standard exists, and the submitted framing inverts the treatment of a diffuse disease
verify.note: No multi-centre prospective series in JTCVS establishing surgical algorithms for DIPNECH could be found, and the submission's clinical claim runs against the disease. It states such a series 'establishes parenchyma-sparing sleeve resections and anatomical segmentectomies as the DEFINITIVE STANDARD, strongly advising against radical lobectomies for multifocal indolent neuroendocrine lesions'. The literature is explicit that there are NO evidence-based management guidelines for DIPNECH; the published surgical experience is case reports and small series of wedge resections and lobectomy; somatostatin analogues are the mainstay for symptom palliation; and resection is considered for individual larger progressive tumours, not for the hyperplasia. Declaring any resection the 'definitive standard' for a diffuse, bilateral, indolent airway process is the wrong shape of recommendation — it would push a surgeon to operate on a disease that is not resectable and whose dominant symptom is medically treatable. Entry rewritten to state the real position, including the parenchyma-conservation argument, which is the one part of the submission's instinct that is sound and which matters precisely because the disease is multifocal. The submission's 'Clinical Guideline Impacts' framing has been dropped: there is no guideline to impact.

title: DOACs Versus Warfarin for Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation After Cardiac Surgery
breakthrough: A meta-analysis of randomised and observational studies totalling 16,902 patients found direct oral anticoagulants associated with lower bleeding risk than warfarin (relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.62–0.89) and fewer major neurological events, with no difference in mortality. A separate synthesis found DOACs associated with lower stroke risk, a trend toward less systemic embolisation, and no increase in readmission, bleeding or mortality. North American registry data show factor Xa inhibitors have been prescribed more often than vitamin K antagonists for postoperative atrial fibrillation since about 2020 — practice moved ahead of the guidelines.
impact: For the patient discharged in atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery, the accumulated comparison favours a DOAC on bleeding and neurological events, without a mortality difference either way — and removes the INR monitoring burden in a patient already managing a complex postoperative recovery.
practical: The unsettled question is not which agent but WHETHER to anticoagulate at all, and for how long: postoperative atrial fibrillation is often transient, the stroke risk attributable to it is not the same as in non-surgical AF, and no trial has established the duration. That is the conversation to have, not the choice of drug. Where a DOAC is chosen, the practical caveats are the ordinary ones and they bite in this population: renal function determines dose and eligibility, a mechanical valve rules DOACs out, and recent pericardial or mediastinal bleeding changes the calculus. Confirm the AF is documented and not a monitor artefact before committing someone to months of anticoagulation.
link: Safety of direct oral anticoagulants compared to warfarin for atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis

verify.status: NOT FOUND as cited — the named study, the length-of-stay figures and the Class I status could not be verified, and the submitted link points at a different document
verify.note: The clinical direction is supported but almost none of the specifics are. (1) No 'comparative study published in The Annals of Thoracic Surgery' evaluating discharge DOAC versus warfarin for POAF with a 'median 7 days vs 9 days' length of stay could be found; that figure is unsourced and has been removed. (2) The submission's LINK is a ResearchGate page for the STS 2026 POAF GUIDELINE — a different document from the one the entry describes, and the same guideline that is entry 1 of this list. A citation pointing at an unrelated paper is a tell this review has seen before. (3) 'Endorsing DOACs as the preferred CLASS I alternative to Warfarin for post-op AF lasting beyond 48 hours' could not be verified as a class assignment. What IS verifiable and has been substituted: a 16,902-patient meta-analysis showing lower bleeding (RR 0.74) and fewer major neurological events with no mortality difference, a second synthesis showing lower stroke risk, and registry evidence that factor Xa inhibitors overtook vitamin K antagonists for POAF from around 2020. Added the question the submission skipped entirely — whether and for how long to anticoagulate transient POAF, which is genuinely unresolved and is the decision that precedes agent choice — plus the renal, mechanical-valve and recent-bleeding constraints.
